Alexia Ntakos: From the Soccer Field to a 225KM Challenge
How a former youth soccer standout turned personal loss into a 225-kilometre fundraising run for cardiovascular research.

Long before Alexia Ntakos challenged herself to run 225 kilometres for cardiovascular research, she was already learning what it meant to lead, adapt and push herself on the soccer field.

In 2017, at just 12 years old, Ntakos was a standout player for the Norval Croatia under-12 girls' soccer team. That summer, her abilities earned her an opportunity to compete on an even bigger stage.

![banner](/images/banner.jpg)

Ntakos was one of six Ontario players selected to join six players from Quebec and form Team Red for the Canadian qualifier of the Danone Nations Cup, the world's biggest international football tournament for children aged 10 to 12. The team travelled to Boucherville, Quebec, where they faced another Ontario-Quebec selection with a spot at the world final on the line.

Team Red won 2-1, earning a place at the Danone Nations Cup World Final at Red Bull Arena in the New York area that September, where they would compete alongside teams representing Italy, France, Spain, the United States and Brazil. Ntakos' performance was particularly memorable. Although she was more naturally a midfielder, assistant coach Patrick Leduc — a former member of Major League Soccer's Montreal Impact — placed her at centre-back. Rather than being discouraged by the unfamiliar position, she embraced the responsibility.

> "Alexia led by example," Leduc said at the time.

![alexia1](/images/alexia1.jpeg)

Late in the match, with Team Red trailing, Ntakos pushed forward into midfield without being instructed to do so. She took a quick free kick that created a breakaway and helped produce the equalizer. She later scored during the penalty shootout to help secure the victory. Ntakos had shown the maturity to adapt, recognize what her team needed and take initiative when the game was on the line.

## A Different Kind of Challenge

That same willingness to step outside her comfort zone has followed her into adulthood.

Years later, Ntakos found herself taking on a very different kind of challenge. Instead of a soccer field, she chose the roads. Instead of competing for a place at an international tournament, she was running to support a cause deeply connected to her family.

![gg](/images/gg.webp)

Her father suffered a heart attack at just 49 years old, an experience that changed the way she viewed cardiovascular disease. She watched him recover and work toward returning to everyday life, while carrying a fear that has remained with her. Her grandfather later experienced severe cardiovascular complications and ultimately passed away following them. Seeing the effects of heart disease on both of them — and on the family around them — made the issue deeply personal.

## 225 Kilometres for a Cause

In March 2026, Ntakos turned that personal connection into action. She challenged herself to run 225 kilometres throughout the month while raising funds for cardiovascular research through the Heart and Stroke Foundation of Canada.

By the end of the fundraiser, she had raised $1,120 toward her $2,000 goal, reaching 56% of her target.

![heart](/images/heart.jpg)

The challenge may have looked very different from the soccer tournament she competed in as a child, but the underlying quality was familiar: a willingness to take on something difficult and keep moving forward.

## Then and Now

At 12, Ntakos was a young midfielder trusted to take on an unfamiliar role and lead her team when it mattered most. Nearly a decade later, she was once again challenging herself — this time for something much more personal.

For Ntakos, the 225KM run was ultimately about turning experiences of fear and loss into something meaningful and helping create a future where fewer families have to experience the same.

Jenna McCallum explores the intersection of music, vulnerability, human connection, and purpose, building an artistic identity rooted in authenticity rather than fame.

For Jenna McCallum, music has never simply been music.

At 21, the Australian vocalist Jenna McCallum has already developed an unusual personal relationship with sound. Before releasing her own music, Jenna has spent years discovering what music can do—not only as an art form, but as an escape, a source of safety, and a way of connecting people who may otherwise have nothing in common.

> "I feel like a major source of relief, comfort, expression was through singing for me," she says.

## Growing Up in Geelong

Growing up in Geelong, Victoria, in Australia, Jenna describes herself as privileged to have been raised by two loving parents who devoted themselves to her. Her childhood, however, was not without its difficulties. Jenna grew up alongside a severely disabled sister, whose needs naturally required a significant amount of attention from the family.

![banner](/images/eve.jpeg)

> "It did shift the focus away from a lot of normal attention needs that a child needs when they grow up, because she needed double of that," Jenna explains.

Her family history is equally layered. Her mother was born in Zimbabwe before eventually moving to Australia, while her father was born in Geelong. Jenna also discovered that one of her great-great-great-grandmothers was among the first prisoners transported to Australia with the First Fleet—and one of only two women from that group to eventually be set free.

That history, combined with her parents' differing backgrounds and beliefs, created an environment where Jenna learned that differences did not have to create division.

Those principles followed Jenna into music.

## Finding Music

![banner](/images/lens.jpeg)

Singing became an outlet from a young age, particularly as she encountered experiences that were difficult to process. Experiences and ups and downs all became part of the complicated emotional landscape that eventually informed her creativity. For Jenna, singing became a form of self-soothing.

> "I think that if I didn't have music, I wouldn't be here." she says.

That statement is perhaps the clearest explanation of why her ambitions extend beyond simply becoming a successful vocalist. Jenna doesn't want to make music that merely sounds good. She wants to create something listeners can inhabit.

> "I want to be an escape for people essentially."

The kind of music she imagines is immersive. She wants listeners to feel as though they are being taken somewhere—to hear a voice that tells them a story, creates visuals and evokes an emotion they might not have known how to express themselves. Most importantly, she wants people to feel safe.

That desire comes from her own experiences with music. Throughout her life, songs and artists have provided the kind of emotional companionship that can be difficult to find elsewhere. As she became more involved in music, she began to recognize that she could potentially offer that same feeling to somebody else.

That is also why Jenna sees music as something fundamentally human. In an era increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence and social media, she believes there will always be something irreplaceable about the connection between one person and another.

## The Universal Language

To Jenna, music is the universal language—not because everyone understands the lyrics, but because everyone can understand emotion. She listens across genres and cultures, from rap and country to classical, rock, punk and heavy metal. Genre, to her, is secondary to execution and feeling.

Her admiration for James Blake illustrates that philosophy particularly well. Blake sits at the centre of Jenna's current musical admiration, particularly because of his production. She is fascinated by his ability to manipulate sound, texture and melody in ways that make music feel almost physical. His work with artists such as Frank Ocean, Travis Scott and Metro Boomin has further reinforced Jenna's appreciation for production that can turn an already powerful vocal or lyric into something atmospheric and unforgettable.

But her influences stretch much further.

Adele and Sia were major influences during her childhood, while artists such as RAYE, Whitney Houston, Kelly Clarkson and Michael Jackson represent the kind of vocal and emotional performance Jenna admires. She isn't interested in music simply because it belongs to a particular genre. She's interested in what happens when an artist can make you feel something.

## How She Creates

![banner](/images/sil.jpeg)

When Jenna creates, lyrics come first. She reads constantly and has a deep appreciation for poetry, language and flow. A single lyric capable of making someone stop and think can be enough to capture her attention. Words, she says, "mean almost everything" to her. From there comes emotion, followed by melody and production. She is drawn toward small vocal details—high-pitched inflections, layered sounds and melodies that become addictive without necessarily being obvious. Production matters just as much. She loves the contrast of emotionally powerful vocals placed over unexpected or beautiful instrumentation.

That combination of lyricism, emotion and sound forms the foundation of the artist she wants to become.

And while Jenna has yet to officially release her own music, she doesn't see that as a reason to wait before defining what she wants her music to mean. She knows she needs to continue developing her songwriting. She knows there is still work to do. But she also knows what she wants the finished product to accomplish.

She wants someone to listen and think:

> "I feel heard, I feel safe, I'm not alone."

That philosophy also explains her frustration with the direction of modern music and the increasing presence of AI. Jenna isn't interested in competing with technology by trying to replicate it. Instead, she wants to emphasize the qualities technology cannot authentically replace: imperfection, soul, vulnerability and human experience. She wants to bring back the kind of music she associates with artists like Adele, Whitney Houston, Kelly Clarkson and Michael Jackson—music that, in her eyes, carried meaning beyond simply making money.

> "They weren't there just to make a buck," she says. "They were there to send a message."

## What Success Means

For Jenna, success has consequently taken on a completely different meaning. She doesn't dream of fame for fame's sake. She doesn't obsess over numbers or how many people she can influence. Her definition of success is much more intimate. If her music helps one person through something difficult, she considers that a victory.

> "If it saves someone's life or if it saves a part of a person... I've won at life."

That mindset is perhaps what separates Jenna's ambitions from the conventional image of an aspiring artist. She isn't particularly interested in being famous. She wants to leave something behind. She wants people, years later, to remember her as someone who mattered to a particular group of people. Someone who changed something. Someone who brought a sense of humanity back into music.

## A Voice for the Voiceless

![banner](/images/rdd.jpeg)

And interestingly, music isn't even her only passion. Alongside her artistic ambitions, Jenna studies biological sciences, with a focus on zoology and microbiology. Her interest in the natural world reflects another part of the same philosophy that drives her music: the desire to care for things that cannot always speak for themselves.

> "I really think that I need to be a voice for the ones who don't have a voice."

That includes animals, but the sentiment extends further. Whether through science, music or simply the relationships she builds with people, Jenna seems driven by the same underlying principle: to make someone—or something—feel less alone. Perhaps that is why her definition of success feels so simple. Jenna isn't chasing a number. She isn't chasing celebrity. She's chasing impact. And before she has even released her first record, she already knows exactly what she wants that impact to feel like.

To feel human, safe, honest and above all, real.

Savia Ashby: Building a New Lane in Pop, One Song at a Time
How Toronto-based singer-songwriter Savia Ashby is blending dark pop, EDM, rock, and powerful vocals into a sound all her own.

For Savia Ashby, music has always been connected to identity. Long before she was writing songs or performing, she was shaped by the values, cultures, and experiences that surrounded her growing up. Now, the Toronto-based singer-songwriter is bringing those influences into her own version of pop – one built around strong vocals, honest songwriting, and a sound that refuses to stay in one category. With her releases But I Might and Juiceboxx, Ashby has already shown two different sides of herself as an artist. One explores vulnerability, while the other embraces confidence and personality. Together, they introduce an artist who is comfortable being both emotionally open and unapologetically herself. ## Roots and Identity Growing up in Canada, Ashby describes her childhood as a supportive and communicative environment. As an only child in a family of three, she was raised in a home where she felt respected and included. That sense of support became one of the foundations behind her confidence – not only as a person but as an artist. Ashby's identity is also shaped by the combination of cultures she grew up around. Her mother's side is Polish, while her father's side is Canadian with Scandinavian roots. Rather than feeling separate, those backgrounds naturally blended together throughout her upbringing. Her father's Canadian influence reflected the environment she lived in, while her mother kept Polish traditions present in their family life. For Ashby, that connection to her heritage continues to influence the way she sees the world. > "Through the Polish-European lens, I have very strong values and I'm proud of my country," she explains. "I feel as though it has made me more resilient and given me a strong connection to other Polish people around me." Those values don't stop at her personal life – they find their way into her music. When asked what parts of herself appear most in her work, Ashby points to the qualities she has carried with her from childhood. > "My strength and resilience does for sure, my confidence as well 100%." ## Finding Music Although singing was always something she loved, music became something more serious when she was 15 years old. That was the point where it shifted from something she enjoyed into something she wanted to pursue as a career. Growing up, Ashby found inspiration in some of pop's biggest names, including Ariana Grande, Selena Gomez, Lady Gaga, and The Black Eyed Peas. Those artists shaped her appreciation for memorable melodies, powerful performances, and music that connects with people. However, inspiration does not mean imitation. Ashby is focused on taking those influences and turning them into something personal. She describes her sound as music for people who want to feel good – confident, energetic, and built around emotion. Her current direction combines dark pop, EDM influences, rock elements, and pop production, while keeping vocals at the center of everything. ## The Creative Process When creating a song, the process begins with meaning. > "First I think of my concept – what is it that I really wanna say? Then I find a beat and vibe, and then I write the lyrics. Production ideas happen as I'm in the studio and we hear cool stuff. We pivot all the time." That willingness to experiment is an important part of Ashby's creative process. Instead of forcing a song into a specific formula, she allows ideas to develop naturally and lets the music evolve along the way. She describes her music as "very fun and vocally focused," a style influenced by the singers she admired growing up, especially Ariana Grande and her ability to combine technical skill with emotion. ## But I Might and Juiceboxx That vocal focus is already present throughout Ashby's releases. But I Might introduced listeners to a more vulnerable side of her artistry, using emotion and honesty as the foundation. The song showed her ability to express personal experiences while creating something relatable. With Juiceboxx, Ashby shifted the energy. The track brings a more playful and confident perspective, using humor and clever lyricism to explore modern dating and emotional immaturity. Instead of moving away from vulnerability, it shows another side of the same artist – one who can be both reflective and fearless. In a genre where many artists can begin to blend together, Ashby believes her voice and songwriting approach help separate her from the crowd. > "I can perform very well vocally, and I think my voice has a uniqueness to it. Also lyrically, I try to be innovative." ## Looking Ahead Looking ahead, Ashby sees herself somewhere between the worlds of artists like Madison Beer and Ariana Grande, while still creating something that reflects her own perspective. > "I think I'll fall into the vein of the more Madison Beer and Ariana Grande route, but I do think I'll create a new section in that area by mixing the dark pop, EDM, vocals, and rock elements." Beyond her releases, Ashby continues building her presence through performances in Toronto and connecting with listeners online through behind-the-scenes studio content, previews, and creative videos that show the personality behind the music. For Ashby, the goal has never been simply to make songs – it has been to create something people can connect with. But I Might introduced her emotional side. Juiceboxx showed her confidence. Together, they represent the beginning of an artist who knows where she wants to go while still leaving room to discover what comes next. Savia Ashby isn't trying to fit into pop music's existing blueprint. She's building one that feels like her own.

From hard-hitting trap to genre-defying artistry — how Toronto's Razi built a career defined by constant evolution.

Few artists develop as dramatically as Razi. Originally performing under the moniker 2x Smokie, the Toronto, Ontario artist has built a reputation by refusing to remain in one lane. Since beginning his musical journey, Razi has consistently reinvented both his sound and artistic identity, evolving from hard-hitting trap records to emotionally driven melodic music, R&B, house, Afrobeats, and multilingual performances. Throughout every era of his career, one quality has remained constant: versatility. Unlike much of Toronto's modern rap scene, which often centers on drill production and themes of violence, survival, and street life, Razi has always approached music differently. While he occasionally explored similar aesthetics and themes early in his career, his focus quickly shifted toward themes of ambition, luxury, personal growth, emotional vulnerability, culture, and self-reflection. His music has become known for its carefully selected production, increasingly sophisticated lyricism, and an ability to move effortlessly between genres without sacrificing authenticity. Born Razi Derrick, throughout the years, Razi's songwriting has matured tremendously. His lyrics have become increasingly layered, incorporating double entendres, triple entendres, and complex wordplay while remaining memorable and accessible. Every release has shown noticeable improvement, reinforcing a pattern that has become synonymous with his career: every hiatus results in a better artist. ## The Beginning (2020–2021) Razi's earliest releases arrived under the name 2x Smokie. His first singles, Branded and Santana, introduced listeners to an artist with undeniable potential. Although both tracks were later removed from streaming platforms — likely reflecting his desire to curate a catalog that better represented his artistic standards — they remain important chapters in his development. In 2020, he released Turn It Up, a breakout moment that immediately showcased his ability to craft infectious hooks over hard-hitting production. # Who is Will Abbass?

Born and raised in Halifax, Nova Scotia, Will Abbass has always been drawn to competitive environments. From an early age, basketball became a major part of his life, shaping not only his identity as an athlete but also the discipline, consistency, and work ethic he would eventually carry into his creative career.

Born in 2006 to a Lebanese father and an English mother, Will grew up between two cultures. His mother's family had lived in the Maritimes for generations, while his father's Lebanese heritage remained an important part of his upbringing. Rather than existing separately, the two cultures naturally blended within his family and everyday life.

His family maintained traditions connected to his Lebanese roots while incorporating elements of their English and Maritime backgrounds. That mixture gave Will an early appreciation for the diversity around him and a curiosity about the ways different cultures could influence one another. Over time, that curiosity became part of how he looks at people, environments, and culture through his own lens.

![pfp](/images/pfp.JPG)

His connection to photography also began before he ever considered it a career. His grandfather ran a photography studio and development plant in Cape Breton for years before Will was born. After his grandfather passed away, photography took on a deeper meaning. It became a way for Will to pay homage to him while continuing a creative legacy in his own way.

Before the camera became central to his life, however, basketball came first.

Standing at 7'0", Will played predominantly at power forward and centre and eventually reached the professional level. Basketball placed him in highly competitive environments from a young age. It demanded discipline, resilience, consistency, and the ability to perform under pressure—qualities that continue to shape how he approaches his creative work. Looking back, Will says he's grateful for everything the sport gave him: the people he met, the opportunities he experienced, and the mentality it instilled in him.

![kneel](/images/kneel.JPG)

Photography was developing alongside all of that.

While still playing professional basketball, Will began taking photography more seriously. What started as a hobby eventually caught the attention of his teammates, who noticed how much he enjoyed being behind the camera and encouraged him to pursue it further.

He had loved taking photographs for as long as he could remember, but stepping away from basketball finally gave him the freedom to explore photography on his own terms. In many ways, the transition brought him back to something that had already been part of his family history. His grandfather had worked behind a camera long before him. Now Will was developing his own relationship with the medium—not simply continuing what came before, but building something distinct from it.

![stu](/images/stu.jpeg)

## Finding His Visual Language

For Will, music has had one of the strongest influences on the way he creates.

Some of his earliest inspirations came from A$AP Rocky and A$AP Mob, Tyler, the Creator and Odd Future, and Westside Gunn and Griselda.
